articles.title: How to teach anything in 60 seconds

body.support:
A good **how-to** reel teaches one thing, fast.

**1. Pick one skill.** Keep it small. Who is it for?

**2. Check your steps.** Look at the instructions or a good website. Then say it in your own words.

**3. Plan it.** Draw each shot in a box:

- **Start:** show the finished thing.
- **What you need.**
- **Steps:** three to five. One step per shot.
- **End:** show it again.

**4. Film it.** Hold the phone up and down. Good light. Film close to your hands.

**5. Cut it.** Get it under 60 seconds. Add the step numbers on screen.

**6. Add captions.** Words on screen help people who can't hear, or have the sound off. Check spelling and full stops.

**7. Your own work.** Use your own video. Don't copy other people's videos. Credit where you checked your steps.

**8. Test it.** Can someone do it after watching?
body.core:
A good **how-to** reel teaches one thing, clearly, fast. Here's how to make one.

**1. Pick one skill, and one audience.** Choose something you can really do, and something people want to learn. Keep it small: *how to change a bike tube*, not *how to fix a bike*. Who's it for? Beginners? Apprentices? Your mates?

**2. Research your steps.** Even if you know how, check a reliable source, like the manufacturer's instructions or a trusted website. Use it to check your steps, then explain them **in your own words**. Note where you checked.

**3. Plan with a storyboard.** Sketch each shot in a box:

- **Hook (0–3 seconds):** show the finished result. *“This is how to get a perfect toastie every time.”*
- **What you need:** tools or ingredients.
- **Steps:** three to five, in order. One step per shot.
- **Finish:** the result again, and a tip.

**4. Film it.** Film vertically. Use good light. Get **close-ups** of your hands. Keep the background tidy. Film each step separately, so it's easy to edit.

**5. Edit it.** Cut anything slow. Get it under 60 seconds. Add text on screen for each step (*Step 1: Remove the wheel*).

**6. Add captions.** **Captions** show what's being said. They help people who are Deaf or hard of hearing, and anyone watching with the sound off. Keep them short. Check **spelling**, **capitals** and **punctuation**, because auto-captions make mistakes.

**7. Use only what you're allowed to.** Use your own footage. Use music you're allowed to use, or none. Don't copy another creator's script or clips: that's **plagiarism**. If you used a source to check your steps, credit it in the caption.

**8. Test it.** Show it to someone who's never done the task. Can they do it after watching? If not, fix the confusing bit.
body.extend:
An effective **how-to** reel teaches a single skill clearly and efficiently. The process mirrors any instructional text: plan, research, draft and edit.

**1. Define scope and audience.** Choose a narrow, achievable skill (*changing a bike tube*, not *bike maintenance*) and a clear audience, such as beginners, apprentices or peers.

**2. Research.** Verify your method against a reliable source, such as manufacturer instructions or an authoritative site. Explain the steps **in your own words**, and record the source.

**3. Storyboard.** Plan each shot: a **hook** (show the result in the first three seconds), what's needed, three to five sequential steps (one per shot), and a finish with a tip.

**4. Film.** Shoot vertically in good light, use **close-ups** for detail, keep backgrounds uncluttered, and capture each step separately.

**5. Edit.** Remove anything that slows the pace, keep it under 60 seconds, and add on-screen step labels.

**6. Caption.** **Captions** make video **accessible** to people who are Deaf or hard of hearing, and to anyone watching on mute. Auto-captions contain errors, so edit them for accuracy, spelling, capitals and punctuation.

**7. Avoid plagiarism.** Use original footage and music you're licensed to use. Don't reproduce other creators' scripts or clips. Credit any source used to verify your method.

**8. User-test.** Have someone unfamiliar with the task follow your reel. Where they struggle, revise.

caseStudies.title: Captions aren't optional

body.support:
Lots of people watch videos without sound.

The government says about **3.6 million Australians** have some hearing loss. By **2060**, it could be **7.8 million**.

Lots of other people watch with the sound **off**: on the bus, or at work.

For them, a how-to video with no captions has no instructions!

There are world rules for online content. They say videos with sound should have **captions**.

Auto-captions make mistakes. So check every caption: spelling, full stops, and saying exactly what you mean.
body.core:
Millions of people watch videos without hearing the sound.

The Australian Government's health department estimates that about **3.6 million Australians** have some hearing loss. As people live longer, it expects that number to about **double**. It could reach **7.8 million by 2060**.

Lots of other people watch videos with the sound **off**. They might be on the bus, in a waiting room, at work, or up late.

For all of them, a how-to video with no captions is a video with no instructions.

There are world rules for making online content work for everyone. They're called the **Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)**. They say videos with sound should have **captions**. Governments and big organisations, including in Australia, use these rules.

Auto-captions help, but they make mistakes. They get names, slang, accents and technical words wrong. In a how-to video, one wrong word can make someone do the wrong thing.

So good creators check every caption. It's a literacy skill: spelling, punctuation, and saying exactly what you mean.
body.extend:
Many people watch video without hearing the sound.

The Australian Government's health department estimates that about **3.6 million Australians** have some hearing loss. As the population ages, that is expected to roughly **double, to 7.8 million by 2060**. Many more people watch with the sound **off**: on public transport, at work, or in shared spaces.

For all these viewers, a how-to video without captions says very little.

The **Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)** are the world standard for making online content usable by everyone. They say pre-recorded video with sound needs captions. Governments and organisations around the world, including in Australia, use WCAG as their benchmark.

Auto-captions help, but they make errors, especially with names, slang, accents and technical terms. In an instructional video, one wrong caption can lead to the wrong action.

So editing captions is a literacy task, not just a technical one. It needs accurate spelling and punctuation, clear sentences and exact wording.

model.text:
**Skill:** How to check your car's oil. **Length:** 60 seconds.

**Hook (0 to 5 s):** “Do this once a month and save your engine.”

**Step 1 (5 to 15 s):** Park on flat ground. Engine off. Caption: “Wait 5 minutes.”

**Step 2 (15 to 30 s):** Pull out the dipstick. Wipe it. Push it back in. A close-up of my hands.

**Step 3 (30 to 45 s):** Pull it out again. The oil should sit between the two marks.

**End (45 to 60 s):** “Low? Top it up, or tell an adult.”

**Captions:** On every step. **Checked with:** the car's manual.

**Test:** My cousin, who has never done it.

teacher.overview: The Online & Safe boss level. Students plan, research, storyboard, film, edit and caption a 60-second how-to reel that teaches one real skill, using their own footage and allowed music, crediting the source used to check their steps, and testing it on a real viewer. They annotate a reel plan, sort what's OK to use, and plan and storyboard their own. The case study is captioning: the Department of Health estimates about 3.6 million Australians have some hearing loss (projected to double by 2060), and the international Web Content Accessibility Guidelines require captions for pre-recorded video with sound.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** the finished result, and a promise of what they'll learn. People who are Deaf or hard of hearing and anyone with the sound off; auto-captions make mistakes. Use your own footage and words; credit sources; use allowed music; don't copy scripts or clips.

**Reel plan:** 1 hook; 2 what you need; 3 close-up with numbered step caption; 4 precise caption; 5 finish and tip; 6 credits (source checked, original music).

**Sort:** own video — OK; another creator's clip — not OK; checked steps in own words with credit — OK; copied script — not OK; friend who agreed — OK; stranger without asking — not OK.

**Case study:** people who are Deaf or hard of hearing, people on public transport or at work with sound off, people learning English; auto-captions make errors with names, slang and technical words; answers will vary.

realityCheck: **Filming eats time.** Keep skills tiny and storyboards tight.
**Students love this.** Expect toasties, hair, sneakers and phone tricks. All fine.
**Caption checking is the literacy core.** Don't let auto-captions slide through unedited.
**Privacy.** Default to class sharing; ask before filming anyone.
**Works in a real class:** yes. A great portfolio piece.
